recipes.title: Loop engineering: /goal and routines
recipes.summary: A loop is three things: do a step, check it against a finish line you wrote down, then go again or stop. /goal runs that loop while you watch. A routine runs it on a timer in the cloud. The hard part, she says, is the checker. Her own checker is the part that breaks your rules.
recipes.one_thing: Her shape for every /goal prompt, from her cheat sheet : Her first demo sorted her Downloads folder into subfolders by type. The prompt ended: "Keep going until no files are left. Do not delete anything. And stop after 30 turns." ( 27:30 ) She names three things that made it a good goal: a clear end state, a check it can run, and a guardrail. The turn limit is her token brake. In July she stretched it to five parts: task, why, outcome, constraints, verification. Verification matters most ( 9:00 ). "actually the hardest part is defining the checker" ( 21:01 )
recipes.try_tonight: This costs no API money, stays on your Mac and touches nothing public. Step 3 is the point. It puts your rule into the loop: the checker's "done" is a claim, and the recount is the evidence.

recipes.title: Live search data in Claude Code
recipes.summary: Two creators plug the same paid data service, DataForSEO, into Claude Code so it can read real search numbers instead of guessing them. The idea is sound. The data is Google's, not Etsy's.
recipes.one_thing: Ask Claude "what do people search for?" and it gives a confident answer from memory. Ryan's point is that the model is not reading live data. "they're not up-to-date 24/7" ( 2:32 ) Connect a data service, and the same question comes back with real columns. His came back with monthly search volume, keyword difficulty and cost per click ( 7:31 ).
recipes.try_tonight: Only if you are choosing the next product. It does nothing for the current zero-sales problem. The prompt: Using only the DataForSEO MCP, get Google search volume in Australia, with a 12-month trend, for these 10 phrases: [your phrases]. Before any paid call, state the endpoint and estimated cost. After it, report the real cost from the API response. Label the result "Google, not Etsy", with today's date. Then search the best two phrases on Etsy yourself, logged out, the way you measured your rankings. The Google number says the need exists. Only the Etsy search says who you'd be up against.

recipes.title: A hook that tells you when Claude is done
recipes.summary: Her Claude Code moos when it finishes. It is a hook: a desktop notification plus a sound, set up by typing one sentence. You already run many hooks, so the setup is not the hard part for you. The hard parts are getting it into the right file, and keeping it from pinging you when a chat is not really done.
recipes.one_thing: Her prompt ( 1:06:30 ): "Set up a hook so my Mac sends me a desktop notification every time you finish a long task." ( 1:06:30 ) It goes on: she wants a sound too, "so I don't need to watch the screen". Hers shows "Cloud Code finished" in the top right corner ( 1:06:30 ) and "plays a moo sound at 46% volume" ( 1:07:00 ). What a hook is, in her words: "when something happens with Claude Code, you can trigger something else to happen." ( 16:31 ) And why it beats remembering: "you don't have to remember to run them. Like they will just happen." ( 1:07:00 )
recipes.try_tonight: This costs nothing and touches nothing public. It changes a settings file, so read the plan before approving it. ⚠ The first macOS notification from a script may need you to allow notifications in System Settings. Glass and Hero are standard Mac sounds (both present in /System/Library/Sounds, checked 16 Sep).

recipes.title: CLAUDE.md built by interview
recipes.summary: Her way to write a CLAUDE.md: let Claude ask you questions one at a time, then have it write down what it learned so you never answer them again. It is aimed at someone with an empty file. Your files are the opposite of empty, so for you the useful version runs the other way: an interview to decide what to cut.
recipes.one_thing: Step one is her lazy-prompt habit. Type the task, then add: "Ask me clarifying questions and one at a time until you're 95% confident you can complete the task." ( 23:31 ) Step two, once the questions are answered: "Create a Claude.md file based on everything you've learned about my preferences and how I work." ( 28:31 ) Her reason is simple: "make sure Claude remembers it so we don't have to do that ever again" ( 27:01 ). She calls the file "the instruction manual for each project", and Claude reads it every time a session starts ( 27:30 , 28:01 ). ⭐ For setting up a real project, she says it
recipes.try_tonight: Read-only. It changes no file. ⚠ Use your strongest model for this. Deciding whether a rule is still needed is a judgement, and your rule keeps Haiku out of judging.

recipes.title: Promo videos made with code: Hyperframes and Remotion
recipes.summary: Both tools let Claude write a video as code, then record it to an MP4 on your own computer. No credits, only plan tokens. They are good at moving text, charts and screenshots. They are also good at drawing a product that does not exist, which is the part you must never use.
recipes.one_thing: Her promise is simple. You describe a video, Claude codes it, and a free tool records it. "it's actually coding a website like using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and then it's like animating that website and recording it" ( 5:30 ) That makes it a promo tool, not an art tool. For you it splits in two: The rule for every video: each product page shown is a PNG rendered from the real PDF, placed in the folder as a media file. The code may move it, crop it and frame it. It may not draw it.
recipes.try_tonight: This costs plan tokens only. It needs no API key, stays on your Mac and posts nothing. Step 5 is the point. The only thing that decides whether this video can ever be used is whether every page in it is a real page.
